question.stem: In an experiment on the photoelectric effect, monochromatic light falls on a metal surface. For each frequency $f$ of the light, the stopping voltage $V_{\text{s}}$ is measured: the smallest potential difference that stops all the emitted electrons from reaching the collecting electrode. The graph shows the results.
question.diagramAlt: Graph of stopping voltage in volts against frequency in units of 10 to the 14 hertz, from 4 to 11. Five measured points lie on a straight line that meets the frequency axis at 5.5 and rises to 2.0 volts at 10.5 and 2.2 volts at 11.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Below a certain frequency, no electrons are emitted however bright the light is. Outline why this observation supports a particle model of light rather than a wave model.
markscheme: In the wave model, energy arrives continuously, so bright enough light of any frequency should eventually release electrons ✓
In the photon model, each electron absorbs the energy of one photon, $E = hf$; below the threshold frequency one photon has less energy than the work function, whatever the number of photons ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: State the threshold frequency of the metal.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine, using the graph, a value for the Planck constant.
markscheme: $eV_{\text{s}} = hf - \Phi$, so the gradient of the graph is $\dfrac{h}{e}$ ✓
gradient read from the line, e.g. $\dfrac{2.0 - 0}{(10.5 - 5.5) \times 10^{14}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{V s}$ ✓
Accept $6.20 \times 10^{-34}$ to $6.60 \times 10^{-34}$ J s. Do not accept the data booklet value without a gradient.

mistakes.feedback: The gradient of the graph is h/e, not h: multiply it by the elementary charge.
That is the data booklet value. The question asks for the value this experiment gives: use the gradient of the graph.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Calculate the minimum energy, in eV, needed to remove an electron from this surface.
markscheme: Allow ECF from (b) and (c); allow the data booklet value of $h$ (giving about 2.3 eV); accept 2.08 to 2.32 eV

parts.label: e
parts.question: The intensity of the light is doubled while its frequency stays the same. Explain the effect, if any, on the stopping voltage.
markscheme: No change in the stopping voltage ✓

The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends only on the photon energy ($hf$) and the work function; more intense light means more photons per second, so more electrons per second, not more energetic electrons ✓

hg.what: value of h the graph was drawn with (an experimental result)

parts.label: a
parts.examinerNote: One mark for what the wave model predicts, one for the photon explanation (one photon, one electron; photon energy depends on frequency only).

parts.label: b
parts.examinerNote: Read where the line meets the frequency axis, remembering the axis unit of 10^14 Hz.

parts.label: c
parts.examinerNote: Rearranging Einstein's equation: V_s = (h/e) f − Φ/e. The line passes through grid points (5.5, 0) and (10.5, 2.0). The experimental h is about 3 % below the accepted value, as in many real experiments.

parts.label: d
parts.examinerNote: Either the graph value of h or the booklet value is fine: the intercept on the voltage axis (extended) also gives −Φ/e.

parts.label: e
parts.examinerNote: The second mark needs the reason, not just "no change". Mention of a larger photocurrent is fine but not required.
